questions.prompt: In Pydantic v2, `class Args(BaseModel): order_id: str = Field(alias="orderId")`, with no model config. What does `Args(order_id="A-1")` do?

choices.text: Creates the model: the field name and the alias are both accepted
Raises `TypeError` for an unexpected keyword argument
Raises `ValidationError`: the field `orderId` is missing
Creates the model with `order_id` left as `None`

questions.explanation: By default Pydantic validates by alias only (`validate_by_alias=True`, `validate_by_name=False`), so the input must use `orderId`; the `order_id` key is ignored like any extra field, and the required field is reported missing. Set `validate_by_name=True` in the model config to accept both. Serialization has the opposite default: `model_dump()` uses field names unless you pass `by_alias=True`.

sources.title: Fields | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: With alias set, validation accepts only the alias by default; validate_by_name=True in the model config is needed to accept the field name as well.

sources.title: Models | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: By default Pydantic ignores extra input keys rather than raising an error.

questions.prompt: `class Run(BaseModel): tags: list[str] = []`. After `r1 = Run(); r1.tags.append("x")`, what is `Run().tags`?

choices.text: `[]`, because Pydantic copies a mutable default for each new instance
`["x"]`, because every instance shares the one default list
Nothing: Pydantic rejects a mutable default when the class is defined
`None`, because a list default needs `Field(default_factory=list)`

questions.explanation: Unlike a plain function default, which every call shares, a Pydantic model makes a deep copy of a non-hashable default such as a list for each instance, so `r1`'s change doesn't leak into later instances. `Field(default_factory=list)` also works, and a factory is the right choice when the default must be computed fresh, such as the current time.

sources.title: Fields | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: When a default value is not hashable, Pydantic creates a deep copy of it for each new model instance, so a list default is not shared between instances.

questions.prompt: `quantity: int` has a `@field_validator("quantity")` with no `mode` argument. The model is validated with `{"quantity": "3"}`. What value does the validator receive?

choices.text: The string `"3"`, exactly as it appeared in the input
The whole input dict, so it can read any field
Nothing: Pydantic rejects the string before any validator runs
The integer `3`, after Pydantic's own parsing has run

questions.explanation: The default mode is `after`: the validator runs after Pydantic's internal validation, so it gets the parsed, type-safe value (lax mode turned the numeric string `"3"` into `3`). Use `mode="before"` to see the raw input, for example to strip or split a string before it is parsed. In either mode the validator must return the value.

sources.title: Validators | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: Field validators default to after mode, which runs after Pydantic's internal validation and receives the already-parsed value; before validators get the raw input, and validators must return the value.

sources.title: Conversion Table | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: In lax mode an int field accepts a numeric-only string such as '3' and converts it.

questions.prompt: `CreateTicketArgs` defines `priority` first, then `due_date`. The rule: an `"urgent"` ticket must have a `due_date`. Where does that check belong?

choices.text: In a `@field_validator("priority")` that reads `info.data["due_date"]`
In a `@model_validator(mode="after")` method that checks `self` and returns it
In a `@model_validator(mode="before")` method that reads `self.due_date`
In any validator, as long as it raises `ValidationError` directly

questions.explanation: An `after` model validator is an instance method that runs once every field is validated, so both values are on `self`: raise `ValueError` if the rule fails and return `self` otherwise. The field validator fails because fields are validated in the order they are defined, so `due_date` isn't in `info.data` yet when `priority` is checked. A `before` model validator receives the raw input and has no `self`, and validators should raise `ValueError` or `AssertionError`, which Pydantic collects into a `ValidationError`.

sources.title: Validators | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: Fields are validated in definition order and info.data holds only already-validated fields; after model validators are instance methods that must return the instance, while before model validators are classmethods receiving raw input.

questions.prompt: When would you use a `field_validator` in `before` mode, a `field_validator` in `after` mode, and a `model_validator(mode="after")`? Give one example of each from a tool's argument model.

model_answer.summary: A `before` field validator cleans up raw input before parsing, an `after` field validator checks one already-typed value, and an `after` model validator checks rules that involve several fields.
key_points: A `before` field validator receives the raw input, so it suits normalising it before parsing, such as stripping whitespace or splitting a comma-separated string into a list
An `after` field validator (the default mode) receives the value already parsed to the field's type, so it suits checks on one field, such as a quantity being positive
A `model_validator(mode="after")` runs once all fields are validated and sees the whole instance, so it suits cross-field rules such as `total` equalling the sum of the line items

Validators report failure by raising `ValueError` (or `AssertionError`), which Pydantic collects into a `ValidationError`, and they must return the value (or, for an `after` model validator, the instance)

questions.explanation: The mode decides what the validator sees. Before parsing you get whatever the caller sent; after parsing you get a typed value; an `after` model validator gets `self` with every field set. Choosing the latest stage that has the data you need keeps validators short and type-safe.

sources.title: Validators | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: Before validators run on raw input ahead of parsing, after validators (the default) receive the parsed value, after model validators see the whole validated instance, and validators signal failure with ValueError or AssertionError.

questions.prompt: In Pydantic v2's default (lax) mode, `class Args(BaseModel): quantity: int; order_id: str`. What does `Args.model_validate({"quantity": "3", "order_id": 42})` do?

choices.text: Returns `quantity=3, order_id='42'`: both values are coerced
Raises `ValidationError` for both fields: types must match exactly
Raises `ValidationError` for `order_id` only: `"3"` is coerced to `3`
Returns `quantity='3', order_id=42`: hints aren't checked at runtime

questions.explanation: Lax mode accepts a numeric string for an `int` field, but a `str` field accepts only strings (and bytes), not numbers, so `42` fails with `Input should be a valid string`. Strict mode would reject `"3"` as well. Pydantic, unlike a plain class, does check the annotations at runtime.

sources.title: Conversion Table | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: In lax Python mode an int field accepts a numeric-only string, but a str field has no conversion from int, and strict mode accepts only an int for an int field.

questions.prompt: A model has the field `at: datetime`. What do `m.model_dump()` and `m.model_dump(mode="json")` return for that field?

choices.text: A `datetime` object, then an ISO 8601 string such as `'2026-09-26T10:00:00'`
An ISO 8601 string both times, since `model_dump` is always JSON-safe
A `datetime` object both times; only `model_dump_json()` converts it
A Unix timestamp integer, then an ISO 8601 string

questions.explanation: `model_dump()` defaults to Python mode and keeps Python objects such as `datetime`, which `json.dumps` can't serialise. `mode="json"` returns only JSON-compatible types, and `model_dump_json()` goes straight to a JSON string. Use one of those when the data goes into an API request or a tool result. Going the other way, `model_validate_json` parses and validates a JSON string in one step.

sources.title: Serialization | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: model_dump() defaults to Python mode, whose output may contain non-JSON-serializable objects; mode='json' returns only JSON-compatible types, and model_dump_json() produces a JSON string.

sources.title: Models | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: model_validate_json() validates a JSON string or bytes payload directly.

questions.prompt: `class GetOrderStatusArgs(BaseModel)` has a docstring, `order_id: str = Field(description="The order's ID")` and `include_history: bool = False`. What is the `required` list in `GetOrderStatusArgs.model_json_schema()`?

choices.text: `["order_id", "include_history"]`: every field is listed
`["order_id"]`: a field with a default is optional
`[]`: fields are required only with `Field(required=True)`
There is no `required` key: that is left to the tool definition

questions.explanation: Fields without a default go in `required`. `include_history` has a default, so it appears in `properties` with `"default": false` but isn't required. The class docstring becomes the schema's `description`, and `Field(description=...)` becomes the property's `description`: that is the text the LLM reads when it decides how to call the tool.

sources.title: JSON Schema | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: In model_json_schema() output, fields without defaults go in required and defaulted fields carry a default; the model description comes from the class docstring or Field(description=...).

questions.prompt: You build a tool definition from `CreateTicketArgs.model_json_schema()`. Explain what in the Pydantic model ends up in the schema the LLM sees, and where that schema goes in the tool definition.

model_answer.summary: The schema's property names, types, `required` list and descriptions all come from the model, and it goes in the tool definition's input-schema field, so the field names, defaults and descriptions are what the LLM reads when it fills in the arguments.
key_points: The schema goes in the tool definition's JSON Schema field: `input_schema` for Anthropic, `parameters` for OpenAI function tools
Each field becomes a property with a JSON type, and fields without a default are listed in `required`
`Field(description=...)` becomes the property's description and the class docstring becomes the schema's description, so they should say what each argument means
Nested models are placed under `$defs` and referenced with `$ref`
Aliases are used as property names by default, so the model's arguments come back under the alias names

questions.explanation: Generating the schema from the same model you validate with keeps the two in step: the LLM is told exactly the shape that `model_validate` will accept. The descriptions matter as much as the types, because they are the LLM's only guide to what each argument means.

sources.title: JSON Schema | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: The generated schema uses aliases as property names by default, puts sub-models under $defs referenced by $ref, lists fields without defaults in required, and takes descriptions from docstrings and Field(description=...).

questions.prompt: A tool call's arguments are `{"quantity": "many"}` for a model with the required fields `quantity: int` and `order_id: str`. What does `model_validate` raise?

choices.text: A `ValueError` for `quantity`, the first field that fails, and it stops there
Two `ValidationError`s, one per field, raised one after the other
A `KeyError` for the missing `order_id`, before `quantity` is checked
One `ValidationError` holding both errors, so `error_count()` is 2

questions.explanation: Pydantic checks every field and raises a single `ValidationError` however many errors it found. `e.errors()` lists each one as a dict with keys such as `type`, `loc` (the field's path), `msg` and `input`: here an `int_parsing` error at `('quantity',)` and a `missing` error at `('order_id',)`. Having every problem in one message is what makes it good feedback: the model can fix them all in one retry.

sources.title: Models | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: Pydantic raises a single exception however many errors it finds, and that ValidationError contains all of them.

sources.title: Error Handling | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: ValidationError.error_count() returns the number of errors and errors() lists each with type, loc, msg and input, with types such as int_parsing and missing.

questions.prompt: Your agent validates each tool call with `Args.model_validate(tool_use.input)`. What should the loop do when that raises `ValidationError`, and why?

model_answer.summary: Catch the error, skip running the tool, and send the error text back as that call's `tool_result` marked as an error, so the model can correct its arguments on the next turn, within a step limit.
key_points: Catch `ValidationError` inside the loop instead of letting it crash the run, and don't execute the tool with bad arguments
Return the error message (such as `str(e)` or a summary of `e.errors()`) as the `tool_result` content for that `tool_use_id`, with `is_error` set to `true` (Anthropic API)
The message names each bad field and what was wrong, so the model can retry with corrected arguments
Cap the retries, for example with the loop's `max_steps`, so a model that keeps failing can't loop forever

questions.explanation: A validation failure is feedback, not a crash. Anthropic's docs say that when a tool request is invalid or missing parameters and you return the error in a `tool_result` with `is_error: true`, Claude will retry 2-3 times with corrections. A specific message, naming the field and the problem, helps far more than a generic "failed".

sources.title: Handle tool calls - Claude Platform Docs
sources.claim: A tool_result carries the tool_use_id, the content and is_error: true for failures, and when a tool request is invalid or missing parameters Claude will retry 2-3 times with corrections before apologizing.

sources.title: Error Handling | Pydantic Docs
sources.claim: str(e) gives a human-readable message and e.errors() a structured list of every validation error, including each field's location and message.
